To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
in cortically blind patients, the ventrolateral pre-frontal cortex is involved in the passive control of the phenomenal experience of affect.

the left ventrolaterally situated prefrontal cortex plays an important role in the passive control of affect in cortically blind patients, by modulating the somatic changes that are triggered by subcortically processed information.

in blindsight, somatosensory processing of visual threat-related information is associated with negative affect, and that this affect is reduced when the same stimulus receives full cortical processing, which is associated with an increase in left ventrolateral activity and a decrease of somatosensory activation.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the neural mechanisms that determine the relationship between the phenomenal experience of affect and the somatic changes that trigger it.
the role of the left ventrolantal prefrontal cortex for the control of negative affective states.

the neural mechanisms that are responsible for the integration of information about subcorticically triggered somatic and cortical stimulus processing, and their contribution to the generation of affective experience.

prefrontal cortex plays a role in passive control of affective experience.
the left ventrolaterl prefrontal cortex has a role in the passive control of affective experience, that is, the control of affective somatic responses that are not under voluntary control.

The main takeaway from our work is that
a ‘feels-like’ component of affect can be modulated by the degree to which a stimulus is processed in the cortex, which may be of relevance for the treatment of affect-related disorders.
a ‘feelin’ is not a simple perception of somatic states, but is rather a complex process that involves integration of somatic states with other information.
affective neuroscience needs to pay more attention to the role of prefrontal cortex, which has often been neglected.
